## Introduction
The introduction briefly describes to the reader 1) the key research question
or knowledge gap that is addressed by the study; 2) the data used for this study; 3) the
methods used to investigate the research question; and 4) the key findings and why they
are important. Three to four paragraphs should be sufficient.

Why do we use multivariate data analysis? When conducting inference through hypothesis testing, we require a factorable degree of uncertainty when dealing with sample data. This likely isn't a big surprise When you have multiple response variables that aren't perfectly correlated, standard confidence intervals do not offer calibrated simultaneous coverage. Confidence regions do offer accurate coverage guarantees in multiple dimensions, but they are challenging to describe and use.


Recall the univariate t-based confidence interval for a population mean:

$$\bar{x}\pm t_{n-1}(\alpha/2)\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$
This confidence interval rejects all values of $\mu_0$ outside of its bounds and accepts all values of $\mu_0$ inside its bounds, corresponding to the null hypothesis $$H_0: \mu=\mu_0$$
A region, $R(\mathbf{X})$ is said to be a 100(1-$\alpha$)% confidence region if, before the sample is selected,
$P(R(X)$ will cover the true $\theta ) = 1-\alpha$

library(mvtnorm)
mu = c(x1=0,x2=0)
Sigma = matrix(c(1, .33,
                 .33, 1), nrow=2)
nrow = 2
ncol = 2
alpha = 0.05
data = rmvnorm(n=n,mean=mu,sigma=Sigma) |>
  as.data.frame()

xbar = colMeans(data)
S=cov(data)

confint_x1 = t.test(data$x1)$conf.int
confint_x2 = t.test(data$x2)$conf.int
Fcrit = qf(1-alpha,df1=p,df2=n-p)
critical_stat = (p*(n-1))/((n-p)) * Fcrit

eig = eigen(S/n)
L = eig$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(eig$values))
theta = seq(0,2*pi, length.out=200)
unit_circle = rbind(cos(theta),sin(theta))
ellipse_pts = t(xbar+sqrt(critical_stat)*L %*% unit_citcle)
colnames(ellipse_pts) = c("x1","x2")
ellipse_df = as.data.frame(ellipse_pts)

confint_x1.
